title: Leo meets Attila (452)
hook: the bishop of Rome goes out to meet the invader, and Attila turns back

segments.voice: Yesterday, Brigid of Kildare, the abbess with open hands. Your line was a cross from rushes.

An army is loose in northern Italy. Attila, king of the Huns, has come down into Italy, and cities are falling behind him. In Rome, the emperor's court has no good answer. Nobody knows whether Rome is next. So a small group sets out north, toward the army, not away from it: two high officials of the empire, and with them the bishop of Rome, a man named Leo, the pope. No soldiers to speak of. Just a delegation walking toward the invader himself.
screen: `AN ARMY IN ITALY.` → `A SMALL GROUP GOES NORTH.` → `THE BISHOP OF ROME.`

segments.voice: The account we lean on comes from Prosper of Aquitaine, a writer of Leo's own time who kept a chronicle. It's short, and it's careful. Prosper says the emperor, the senate and the Roman people looked for a plan, and none seemed better than sending envoys to the savage king to ask for peace. So Leo went, trusting in God's help, Prosper says, with the two officials beside him. Next, the meeting. Prosper says Attila received the envoys well, and was so pleased by the presence of the high priest that he ordered the fighting to stop. He promised peace and went back beyond the Danube. That's it. No speech is recorded. No threats, no miracles. A bishop walked out, met a conqueror, and the conqueror turned around. Now, the legends. Later centuries weren't satisfied with something so quiet. A later story says that as Leo spoke, the apostles Peter and Paul appeared above him with swords drawn, and Attila took fright. Prosper says nothing of it. Some readers also note that other writers of the time mention hunger and sickness in Attila's army, which may have helped him decide. We don't know everything that was in Attila's mind. We only know what Leo did: he went out. When everyone else was asking how to keep the danger away, Leo walked toward it. Catholics remember him as Saint Leo the Great, a pope and a teacher of the Church. It wasn't a battle he won. It was a meeting he showed up to.
screen: `PROSPER'S SHORT ACCOUNT.` · `ATTILA RECEIVES THEM.` · `THE LEGEND ADDS SWORDS.` · then, large: `HE WENT OUT.` · then: `A MEETING HE SHOWED UP TO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one conversation you've been avoiding, a call to return, a talk with someone you love, a meeting at work, and without solving it, walk toward it in your mind the way Leo walked north. Notice where your body tightens, the jaw, the shoulders, the stomach, and let it soften a little on each breath out as you picture yourself sitting across from the other person, steady, listening first. If you pray, ask God for calm before that meeting.
pax. Latin for peace, what Prosper says Attila promised Pope Leo before turning his army back from Rome. Today's word.
Your line: he went out. Showing up can be its own kind of courage. That's day seven hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church keeps the feast of Pope Saint Leo the Great, honoring him as a Doctor of the Church, and his meeting with Attila is told as part of his story.

chat.meaning: Prosper of Aquitaine's short account says Attila received Leo well and promised peace. The swords of Peter and Paul come from a later legend.

notes: Prosper's Chronicle: the emperor, senate and people judge nothing better than an embassy; Leo goes 'trusting in God's help' with the consular Avienus and the prefect Trygetius; Attila receives them well, is pleased by the presence of the high priest, stops the war, promises peace and goes back beyond the Danube. Paraphrased; confirm wording, and that 'the most feared man in the world they knew' in the hook is acceptable as narration.

Year 452 is the index title; not used in voice.
